response.content:
Prince Leo had barely passed through the city gate when a voice cut through the din of the crowd.

"Prince Leo! Prince Leo!"

A stocky young man shouldered his way past a merchant's cart, nearly knocking over a basket of turnips in his haste. He was chubby, with a round face flushed red from exertion, and though Leo did not immediately place him, there was something familiar in those features.

Then it clicked. Lord Daren Berwick—son of Duke Noah Berwick, the ruler of this duchy. Leo had met him years ago at an imperial gathering, though the boy before him now looked rather different from the gangly youth he remembered. Despite the difference in their stations—Leo ruling over a small principality at the far end of the Empire while Noah Berwick governed one of its largest duchies—the two had never regarded each other with the deference or presumption that typically accompanied such a gap. They had been boys of the same age, and that had been enough.

"Daren," Leo said, as the lord reached him, breathing hard. "What—"

"Not here." Daren seized his sleeve and pulled him away from the crowd, away from the wagons and foot traffic streaming through the gate. His grip was tight, his hand unsteady. When they reached a quieter stretch of wall, he turned to face Leo, and his voice dropped to barely above a whisper.

"There's been an emergency."

The words came out low, and slightly trembling.

"My father is dead."

Leo stared at him.

"My mother has been taken hostage. In our own mansion." Daren's jaw tightened. "I sent soldiers in to rescue her. They haven't come back. Presumably... they're dead."

Leo glanced at the guards trailing behind him, then back at Daren. "What happened? How did the captors get into your mansion in the first place? What were the guards doing?" He paused. "And how is this something I can help with?"

Daren swallowed.

"The captor is only one person." He held Leo's gaze. "General Sion von Haugwitz."

The name landed like a stone in still water.

"I watched your duel," Daren continued, his voice urgent now. "At the Battle of Pyskov. I saw you stand against him. You nearly beat him."

Leo did not answer immediately. Of course he remembered that duel. He remembered it in his body before he remembered it in his mind—the weight of his sword arm gone numb, the taste of blood in his mouth, the sky wheeling overhead as he lay on his back in the mud. And then Sion, who had been only a captain then, standing tall above him, the great polearm resting against his shoulder like it weighed nothing at all. His life had flashed before his eyes in those long seconds, lying there at the other man's mercy.

"I wasn't anywhere near beating him," Leo said flatly. "He could have killed me if he'd wanted to."

"Perhaps. But you're alive." Daren stepped closer. "Prince Leo, you are the only man alive who has ever dueled Sion von Haugwitz on a battlefield. Every other man who has faced him is dead."

Leo's brow furrowed. Sion had been captured over a year ago during the siege of Sol-Osto. He had heard the reports himself—a prisoner of war, held in custody. How in the world had he ended up here, in the Berwick mansion, taking a duchess hostage?
